demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
avoid anything that could be stressful
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I can no longer trust my own body
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette:
Mateo describes the last six months as living in someone else's body. The person he was before-confident, skilled, proud of his hands and the complex machinery he could command-seems like a character from a story he once read. The memory of the day that changed everything feels similarly detached, like a film clip that plays on a loop in his mind but belongs to a different person. He can see the brilliant summer sun glinting off the rooftop unit, hear the low hum of the condenser, and see his senior partner, Javier, laughing at a joke he'd just made. Then there's the flash, the acrid smell of ozone and burnt wiring that sometimes ambushes him when he opens his own toolbox, and the terrible silence that followed the electrical arc. When the memory forces its way into his mind, uninvited, it's this sudden, unnatural quiet that he finds most terrifying. It's a silence he has come to believe is the sound of disaster unfolding.

In the weeks following the accident, Mateo began a relentless process of self-interrogation. Night after night, he would lie awake, going over every single detail, every turn of a screw, every word exchanged with Javier. He was certain that if he just replayed it enough times, he could pinpoint the one moment, the one fatal oversight, that led to Javier's severe burns. This mental ritual offered no clarity, only a deepening conviction of his own guilt. He felt he would never be able to forgive himself for not doing more, for not being better, for not somehow preventing the inevitable. This belief has become the central truth of his new life. The person he is now, this hesitant and frightened young man, is unrecognisable to him, a stranger who has taken up residence in his skin.

His work as an HVAC technician, once a source of pride, is now a landscape of potential threats. The world has shrunk to a few known locations where he feels a semblance of safety: his small apartment, his truck, and the supply warehouse. Any job site feels perilous. An unexpected quiet, like a compressor cycling off without warning, can make the hair on his arms stand up and his heart hammer against his ribs. He feels his own body betraying him in these moments, the sweat on his palms and the tremor in his hands confirming his deepest fear: that he can no longer trust himself to do his job safely. As a result, he has started avoiding anything that might be stressful. He turns down complex commercial jobs, making excuses to his boss, and sticks to simple residential filter changes. The consequence was a formal warning last month; his career is now as precarious as his sense of self.

His social life has evaporated along with his confidence. He avoids his friends, certain they can see the failure written all over him. The calendar has also become a source of dread. The twenty-first of each month, the date of the accident, is a day he spends in his apartment, curtains drawn, avoiding calls and the possibility of any reminder. He has come to believe that safety is only possible through constant vigilance and radical avoidance. This shrinking life, however, has become its own kind of prison. It was after he found himself unable to even enter a client's basement, frozen on the top step by the unfamiliar quiet and the enclosed space, that he finally made the call. He came to therapy not out of hope, but out of a dawning terror that if something doesn't change, the person he used to be will be gone for good, leaving only this ghost who is too afraid to live.
